frameworks.title: Word order: SOV
frameworks.body: Japanese ends sentences with the verb. 'I sushi eat' (私は寿司を食べる). The particle は marks topic, を marks object.

frameworks.title: Particles do the heavy lifting
frameworks.body: Tiny words like は, を, に, で tell you what role each word plays. Word order is flexible — particles aren't.

frameworks.title: Three writing systems
frameworks.body: Hiragana (native), Katakana (foreign), Kanji (Chinese characters). Learn hiragana first — you can survive on it alone.

frameworks.title: Politeness levels
frameworks.body: Casual (食べる), polite (食べます), honorific (召し上がる). Use the wrong one and you'll seem rude or weirdly formal.

primer.title: How Japanese is written
primer.tagline: Three systems at once, in the same sentence.

facts.label: Hiragana
facts.text: 46 characters, each a full syllable rather than a single sound. Grammar, endings and native words. This is what this course teaches, and it is where everyone starts.

facts.label: Katakana
facts.text: The same 46 syllables in a second, angular set — used for foreign words, names and emphasis. コーヒー is 'coffee'.

facts.label: Kanji
facts.text: Thousands of Chinese characters carrying meaning rather than sound. About 2,000 are needed for a newspaper, and they are learned over years, not weeks.

facts.label: No spaces
facts.text: Japanese does not put spaces between words. The mix of three scripts is what shows you where words begin and end.

primer.hardest: There is no way around kanji, and no shortcut. The good news is that hiragana alone lets you read children's books, menus with furigana, and every grammatical ending in the language.
primer.firstWin: Each kana is one syllable, always pronounced the same way. Japanese has no tones, no genders, and five clean vowel sounds — the pronunciation is genuinely easy.

confusables.tell: Nearly the same shape. き has an extra crossbar — and this is the pattern to expect: hiragana distinguishes many pairs by a single stroke.
Both are two strokes with a hook. ら hooks inward at the top right; わ has a full vertical on the left.
